title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Nessel demands answers on data center power deals and what it means for your electric bills.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're digging into Attorney General Dana Nessel's move today to demand answers from the Public Service Commission on how it's handling those massive power deals for proposed data centers.
Right, and this feels like it's tapping into something bigger that's been building for a while now.

Exactly. Nessel is pressing the PSC to justify its approach to surging electricity demand from these projects, warning that residents could see higher utility bills if regulators greenlight large new loads without stronger oversight.
So why is this coming up now? What's the history here with data centers and the grid?

Data centers have been ramping up proposals across the state for a couple years, drawn by cheap land and power availability. Utilities like DTE and Consumers Energy have been fielding requests for hundreds of megawatts at a time, which is way beyond typical industrial loads.
And the PSC is the one that approves those rate cases and big load additions, right?
Yes, and Nessel's letter today signals she's concerned the commission might be moving too fast without enough scrutiny on who pays for upgrades and how rates get adjusted.
What does that actually mean for people's electric bills if these deals go through unchecked?

The big risk is that new infrastructure costs get spread across all ratepayers, not just the data center operators. A single gigawatt-scale campus can require hundreds of millions in transmission and generation upgrades, and those expenses eventually show up in monthly statements.
I've heard water is another big piece too. How does power tie into that?

Cooling these facilities takes enormous amounts of water, so the same utilities under strain for electricity are also dealing with water system demands. Any new cluster will lean on those same networks.
And farmland and towns? How are those impacted in the bigger picture?

Many proposals target rural areas with open land, which can mean converting farmland and adding traffic and noise. Local governments have been pushing back with zoning changes because they see the long-term costs landing on residents.
Who are the main players besides Nessel and the PSC?

The utilities themselves, data center developers, and increasingly local officials and residents in places like Washtenaw and Cass counties. It's become a statewide conversation about balancing economic development with infrastructure limits.
What happens next after this letter from Nessel?

The PSC will likely have to respond with more detailed justifications or new rules on how they evaluate these loads. It could slow some approvals or force developers to cover more of the upgrade costs upfront.
Is this the first time we've seen this level of pushback from the attorney general's office?
It's one of the strongest signals yet from state leadership that the growth isn't going unchecked. Earlier this week we saw voters and primaries reflecting the same concerns at the local level.
So this could set a precedent for how future projects get reviewed?
That's the hope from critics. Stronger oversight might mean fewer surprises on bills and more transparency on exactly what these facilities will draw from the grid and water systems.
Any sense of how many projects are currently in the pipeline?
Dozens of proposals statewide, with several in southeast Michigan alone. The PSC has been handling them case by case, but today's move suggests they may need a more coordinated framework.
What about emissions and on-site power alternatives that came up in other stories today?

Those are part of the same conversation. Some developers are pitching behind-the-meter generation to bypass grid delays, but that raises its own questions about air quality and noise that regulators will have to weigh.
Bottom line for listeners thirty or sixty miles away who aren't near a proposed site?
Your electric bill and water rates could still be affected because the grid is interconnected. What gets approved in one corner of the state ripples outward.
And if the PSC tightens up, does that mean projects get canceled or just delayed?
Probably a mix. Some may find ways to pay for their own infrastructure or scale down, while others might relocate or wait for clearer rules.
This feels like it's shifting from local zoning fights to state-level policy.
That's the evolution we're seeing. Nessel's involvement brings it into a broader regulatory arena.
How soon could we see changes from this?
The PSC response could come in weeks or months, depending on how they prioritize it. In the meantime, developers and utilities are watching closely.
Thanks for laying that out. Let's move to some of the other stories from today and this week.
OpenAI offered help today hardening cybersecurity on Michigan water utilities after a hack tied to data center growth strains.
That's interesting because any new data center cluster will depend on those same utilities. What does the offer actually involve?
Technical assistance on security protocols for systems already under pressure from AI power and water demands. It's a direct response to a recent attack that exposed vulnerabilities.
Next up, a Michigan firm is pitching on-site power generation to dodge grid delays for AI campuses.
They say they can deliver the massive loads without waiting on utility upgrades, mirroring tactics used elsewhere, but it raises questions about emissions and who pays when the grid is strained.
Detroit released new rules today after a report showed data centers could add hundreds of megawatts on an already tight grid.
The assessment flags impacts even for suburbs thirty miles away served by DTE, and the rules would set size limits plus require developers to pay for upgrades.
Yesterday in Dowagiac, neighbors complained about nonstop noise from a Cass County facility.
Residents describe constant sound with no immediate fix from local officials, showing the quality-of-life costs that hit after projects are built.
On Thursday, Pittsfield Township started tightening zoning near Ann Arbor to curb sprawl, noise, traffic, and power demand.
Those changes could become a template for other Washtenaw County townships and affect future projects.
Wednesday saw Monroe Township moving to dismiss a three-hundred-million-dollar lawsuit over its data center ban.
The case tests whether locals can block projects drawing heavy power and water, with southeast Michigan residents having a stake in the outcome.
Also Wednesday, a data center opponent won a Democratic primary for state House.
That victory moves the debate into the legislature for that district.
Voters near Ann Arbor rejected a billion-dollar rezoning on Wednesday too.
The decision blocks large-scale development that would have used heavy power and water, protecting local farmland and infrastructure.
And in the congressional primary, Will Lawrence defeated Haley Stevens in MI-7 after campaigning against data centers.
That shifts the fight over power demand and tax breaks into Congress for Washtenaw and surrounding counties.
Quite a week of pushback at multiple levels.
It is. Now for on deck.
We didn't spot any public meetings on data center topics scheduled for tonight or tomorrow based on available agendas.
We'll keep monitoring township boards and the PSC calendar and update you if anything pops up.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: AG Nessel Presses PSC on Data Center Power Deals That Could Raise Bills
